column1: # Numeral / nominal classifier inventory of Hmong (White Hmong and Green Mong)
#   White, Nathan M. (2021). The Hmong language of North Queensland.
#   PhD thesis, James Cook University, Townsville. DOI: 10.25903/f5rd-s089.
# Source chapter: ch. 7 "Classifiers" (printed pp. 299-383), with supporting
# PAGE OFFSET CONVENTION: the PDF has 742 pages and a 37-page front matter
# offset, so printed page + 37 = PDF page (printed 303 = PDF 340). All page
# numbers in the PAGE column are PRINTED page numbers as in the thesis.
#   FORM            classifier form in the Romanized Popular Alphabet (RPA),
#                   exactly as the thesis spells it; spaces separate syllables
#   DIALECT         WH = White Hmong, GM = Green Mong, both = the thesis gives
#                   a single form for both varieties. Where White gives a
#                   WH/GM pair (e.g. "WH li/GM le") there are two rows.
#   WHITE_CATEGORY  White's own subclass, lowercased with underscores:
#   CLASS           mapping onto the five classes of Bond & Paik (2000) used
#                   by wordnet: sortal, event, mensural, group, taxonomic.
#   DEFINITION      one clause built from White's own description.
#   EXAMPLES        semicolon-separated "hmong noun (english gloss)" pairs from
#                   his examples, with the classifier STRIPPED (from "lub
#                   none. EXCEPTION: for verbal_action rows the items are the
#                   co-occurring VERBS he lists (Table 38, p. 370), not nouns,
#                   because verbal action classifiers classify events.
#   PAGE            printed page(s) where the form is described.
# WHERE THE BOND & PAIK MAPPING IS A POOR FIT (flagged here, not in a column)
#   - li / le (possessed): mapped to sortal, but White states it "lacks a clear
#     semantic parameter by which to classify" (p. 302) and is a pure default
#     possessive linker. It classifies nothing; no Bond & Paik class fits.
#   - sab/saab, ntav/nta/ntaav/ntaa, tog (locational): mapped to sortal, but
#     White says they combine "inherent arrangement or configuration" with
#     "partitivity as a kind of quanta" (p. 350), i.e. they behave more like
#     mensural/partitive classifiers than like sortal ones.
#   - cov (non_singular): mapped to group, correct for its older 'bunch, group'
#     sense, but its dominant modern value is abstract non-singular/definite
#     with no group semantics - effectively a plural marker (pp. 354-357).
#   - tej (non_singular): mapped to group, but its value is partitive 'some'
#     (part of a whole), which is closer to mensural than to group.
#   - qhov (sortal): a DEFAULT classifier with no semantic parameter; White
#     notes it "adopts mensural-like semantics" with mass nouns (p. 326).
#   - pawg (collective): group with count nouns, but a mensural 'pile'
#     classifier with mass nouns (p. 371-372, glossed CL:PILE).
#   - zaum / zaus (time): counts occasions/repetitions of an event, so `event`
#   - nplooj, kab/kaab, sob: White presents these only in Sec. 7.8.4 (Tables
#     39-40, pp. 381-382) without assigning them to a subclass; the
#     WHITE_CATEGORY `mensural` here is my inference from their semantics
#     (they unitise paper and speech, like nqe, lo, phau, tsab).
#   - "WH khawv 'CL:BITE'" (Table 34, p. 337) occurs exactly once in the whole
#     thesis and is never discussed in prose, so the final <v> (and thus the
#     tone) could not be cross-checked. The repository stopword list has the
#     form `khaw`. Recorded as White prints it: khawv. UNCLEAR.
#   - "WH riam/GM rag 'VCL:CHOP'" (Table 38, p. 370). `rag` is very probably
#     the tone-melody-alternated (Sec. 2.3.1, p. 62) GM form appearing after
#     tuab- 'single', i.e. the citation form would be GM *ram; on p. 402 the
#     same item is printed "WH riam/GM riag 'VCL:STRIKE.WITH.KNIFE'", which is
#     inconsistent with Table 38. Recorded as printed in Table 38. UNCLEAR.
#   - Forms produced ONLY by the lexical tone melody alternation of Sec. 2.3.1
#     (<j>,<s>,<m> -> <g>; <v> -> bare; bare -> <s>) are NOT given rows of
#     their own, because they are inflected variants, not separate classifiers:
#     daig (= daim, p. 174), riag (= riam, pp. 369-371, 402), nploog
#     (= nplooj), ntsug (= ntsuj), teg (= tes), tug (after ib-/ob-), -co
#   - "family" (pp. 342-343) is an English borrowing that White analyses as a
#     genuine collective mensural classifier in diaspora Hmong. He does not
#     label the dialect of examples (596)-(598); recorded as `both`. UNCLEAR.
#   - zaum: Sec. 7.2.4 (p. 345) lists it unmarked for dialect, but Sec. 8.2.1.8
#     (p. 409) gives the pair "WH zaum/GM zaus 'CL:TIMES'". Two rows are given
#   - phau: White writes "WH phau/GM phau/phoo", i.e. the same form in both
#     varieties plus a GM variant. Recorded as one `both` row (phau) plus one
#   - pob 'CL:BALL / CL:PACK' (p. 331) appears only inside an example of the
#     apportioning construction and is not assigned to a subclass; recorded as
#     mensural, from a White Hmong example. UNCLEAR.
#     DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED: White states they are "not part of the system of
#     noun categorization" (p. 366) and they fail his mensural-classifier
#   - Classifiers glossed only in the interlinear appendix texts (e.g. npaug
#     511, feem 'CL:PART' p. 385) are excluded as outside ch. 7.
#   - No source text was OCRed: the PDF carries an embedded text layer, so RPA
#     tone-bearing final consonants were read directly and cross-checked
#     against the surrounding prose wherever prose exists.
